title: Japan’s JR East reveals new train company mascot character, online comments aren’t kind
description: Filling the Suica Penguin’s shoes isn’t going to be easy. JR East/East Japan Railway Company hit a home run when it picked the original mascot for its Suica prepaid card system. Introduced at the same time as the system itself in 2001, the Suica Penguin was an instant success, giving a cute, approachable persona to […]
content:
Filling the Suica Penguin’s shoes isn’t going to be easy.

JR East/East Japan Railway Company hit a home run when it picked the original mascot for its Suica prepaid card system. Introduced at the same time as the system itself in 2001, the Suica Penguin was an instant success, giving a cute, approachable persona to what was at the time a novel way to pay for train fare and shopping purchases. In the two and a half decades since, the popularity of both Suica and its mascot have grown and grown, so it was a shock to many when, one year ago, JR East said it would be replacing the penguin with a new mascot.

▼ So long, Suica Penguin

With the Suica system having become deeply integrated in so many people’s daily lives, the changeover is a big deal. JR East started by having a selection committee sift through artist proposals, then picking out three finalists which were revealed in September, with the winner to be decided through online voting. The candidates were a squirrel…

…a rabbit…

…and some kind of large-eared creature with a mole-like companion riding in its satchel.

Polling ran from September 8 to September 23. JR East has now released the results, and the new Suica mascot is…

…the rabbit…-ish-looking thing.

This doesn’t appear to have been a narrow win, either. Out of a total 1,664,399 votes, 860,152 were for the rabbit. That’s 51.6 percent of the total, so unless one of the losing candidates got hardly any votes at all, the rabbit won by a substantial margin.

This doesn’t mean, though, that everyone is emotionally onboard with the rail company’s new mascot. Reactions to the announcement tweet from JR East have been almost entirely negative, with many calling the character, with its vacant, expressionless eyes and seemingly pasted-on smile, far more creepy than cute. The purple color is also an issue for many, seeing as how it’s an attention-grabbing hue with no connection to JR East’s standard color designs (the company’s image color is green), and to many it looks like the character is suffering from poisoned status in an RPG video game.

“That rabbit is seriously poisoned.”
“Poison Bunny.”
“Has me thinking of the Grimace Shake.”
“Lo, I can feel only darkness within it.”
“Man, they’re really going with the purple one…”
“Was hoping for anything but this.”
“This isn’t cute, and I can’t really tell what it’s supposed to be.”
“I love it. For real. It’s cute.”
“The penguin was cuter.”
“It’s got a Teletubby kind of thing going on, and it’s freaking me out. Should have stuck with the penguin.”
“Looks like some sort of monster from a horror video game.”
“Yep, definitely gonna be some crying kids [when they see the character] at the station.”

／
Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターが決定しました
～お客さまから愛称を募集します～
＼

2026年9月、Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターのデザイン候補3案を発表し、お客さま投票を実施した結果、総得票数1,664,399票のうち860,152票を獲得したのキャラクターに決定しました… pic.twitter.com/LX5RMveCHE

— JR 東日本ニュースリリース【公式】 (@JREast_News) November 18, 2026

The discrepancy between the rabbit being the clear favorite in voting but hardly anyone seeming to have anything to say about the design is surprising. One commenter wondered if the apparent landslide victory was a result of votes from those earnestly wanting a more conventionally cute character being split between the other options, while everyone wanting something weird or casting their vote as a joke then latched onto the rabbit with the unsettling expression. It’s also possible that the somewhat unfinished look of the squirrel (which lacks a visible outline) and the vagueness of the mole-and-friend design prevented them from really resonating with people wanting a conventionally cute mascot.

Of course, there is precedent for a mascot who’s initially seen as creepy-looking to win over the public. When the Osaka Expo 2025 made its mascot a lump of irregularly shaped tissue and eyeballs, more than a few people were shocked, but Myaku-Myaku has gone on to build a fanbase, even after the event’s finish. A major shift in public opinion came after Myaku-Myaku’s voice, and association personality, was added, and there’s a possibility for the new Suica mascot to follow the same playbook. JR East is currently accepting suggestions for the new character’s name through its website here, and the form also includes sections for submitters to write what kind of personality they want the rabbit to have.

Suggestions are being taken between now and December 15. Unlike with the mascot design, though, there will be no public voting this time, and instead the name will be selected by JR East. That’s probably for the best, since as of right now the most common suggestions online seem to be Bian (Japanese for “Option B,” as the rabbit was designated at its initial reveal), and Doku Usagi, which, as you can probably guess, means “Poison Bunny.”

title: FamilyMart’s “physical AI” robot workers getting chilly reception in Japan
description: Sure, it doesn’t do much, but it’s a robot! Even as AI is still in its early stages, many eager start-ups are looking at the next big thing, which they have dubbed “physical AI.” That really just means robots controlled by AI, but it seems to be a buzzword that piggybacks on the name recognition […]
content:
Sure, it doesn’t do much, but it’s a robot!

Even as AI is still in its early stages, many eager start-ups are looking at the next big thing, which they have dubbed “physical AI.” That really just means robots controlled by AI, but it seems to be a buzzword that piggybacks on the name recognition of “AI” itself.

In Japan, one company that has made great strides in actually putting physical AI to the test in real-world applications is Telexistence. Over the past few years, they have been developing robots to alleviate the labor shortages many convenience stores have been facing.

After a fair bit of testing, major convenience store chain FamilyMart announced that, starting next year, they would begin rolling out physical AI drink stockers to every location in Japan. These are AI-powered mechanical claws that are installed behind the drink section and constantly refill cans and bottles.

コンビニ大手のファミリーマートは、飲料を自動で補充するフィジカルAIを活用したロボットを本格導入する方針です。どんなロボットなのでしょうか。https://t.co/LvhlAmeiUY#nhk_video pic.twitter.com/iNwK0u3i5u

— NHKニュース (@nhk_news) November 12, 2026

Watching this system in action, two things are certain to spring to mind. First, it’s quite slow, but realistically, that should be fine since, unlike a human who would pop in and fill everything at once in a couple of minutes, this thing is working nonstop, around the clock. As long as it outpaces the rate people are buying drinks, it should be fine.

The more problematic observation is that the robot is moving drinks from a shelf to the fridge, which begs the question of how that first shelf was stocked. If a human is required to fill the shelf used by the robot to move the drinks into the fridge, then why not get the human to just stock the fridge directly?

According to FamilyMart, adoption of this system will reduce a human’s beverage stocking time by 70 percent. However, since beverage stocking is just one part of an employee’s many duties, it’s unclear how much real-world work that would equate to. Many readers of the news online were unconvinced it would amount to much in comments. People from both inside the industry and out came forward in saying they felt these machines have failed to impress.

“The shelves are restocked by robots from shelves restocked by humans. That’s called doing the same work twice.”
“It has to be fully automated, starting with opening the cardboard boxes. Otherwise, it’s pointless!”
“Why not just make it a big vending machine, where you push a button and the drink comes out?”
“I’m curious about how deliveries are handled, but more importantly… IT’S SOOOOOO SLOW!”
“I was thinking this was a good idea because part-timers sometimes do horrible things. But someone could just hack into these and make them do horrible things too.”
“It’s slow, but if it runs automatically all the time, I guess that’s fine. Guess I’ll be able to take my time at work a little more.”
“I’ve worked with this robot before. I have to restock the shelves behind it, putting a set number of items in specific spots. It’s such a pain in the butt. The rails on the floor it uses are dangerous for humans to trip on. It bugs out a lot, and each time I have to use an iPad or call someone. Humans are faster, and it was such a waste I was literally crying.”
“That is 100 times slower than I even expected.”
“Is there a need for the robotic arm? Why not just tilt the shelves to slide new bottles in?”
“I am the owner of two FamilyMart franchise stores. I think the installation cost for this machine is 1.2 million yen. Considering most stores don’t even generate a net profit of 100,000 yen a month, how could any store afford these? None of the stores are asking for this stuff. The priority should be helping franchises who are struggling with soaring labor costs!”
“I laughed at the ‘physical AI’ part. It’s neither physical nor AI.”

In defense of the people behind these robots, from what I’ve read, this is just one component of a much more integrated system that manages various aspects of running a convenience store, from cleaning floors to managing inventory. Perhaps when viewed as a whole, it would be more useful.

▼ Their bag bot looks promising, but still has a way to go.

Unfortunately, that important detail required extra research to find out, so to most readers it appears as if this single claw was being triumphantly paraded out as the solution to all convenience stores’ problems.

Honestly, I feel like if they’d stuck with the giant cat-man design they started with, it would have gotten a much warmer reception overall.
